extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of Euclidean geometry (readers of Euclid Book III); mathematicians studying classical proofs and their rigor
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and implicit standards for producing and assessing classical Euclidean proofs and constructions concerning circles (Book III), including handling of cases, justified assumptions, and standard constructions (tangents, centres, intersections). Useful for checking completeness and Euclidean style rigor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Take the most obscure case for proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Euclid's manner is to take the most obscure (hardest) case for a proof and leave simpler cases to the reader: "taking the most obscure case for proof and leaving others to the reader."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When proving a proposition, present the most difficult/obscure configuration explicitly; simpler or special placements may be omitted as they follow easily. Note when an author departs from this practice (and whether that departure is justified).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unsupported logical inferences; prefer direct proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Euclid generally does not allow himself purely logical inferences of the form 'every A is B, hence every not-B is not-A'; he prefers to give a new proof rather than rely on such contraposition without demonstration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on informal contraposition or meta-logical steps without providing a geometric proof. If making a logical inference, either cite an earlier proven theorem that provides the inference or give an explicit geometric argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not introduce unproved geometric assumptions (e.g., intersections)
rubrics_metrics.description: Beware unproved assumptions used in proofs — for example, "Euclid's proof contains an unproved assumption, namely that the lines bisecting HQ, BH at right angles will meet in a point F."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly justify existence/uniqueness of intersection points used in arguments (e.g., intersection of perpendicular bisectors). If a construction is asserted, supply or cite a proposition guaranteeing its existence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider all positional/degenerate cases (inside/on/outside)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs must contemplate alternative placements of constructed points (e.g., a point might fall within an angle or on the circumference) and handle those cases or explain why they can be left to the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a construction or argument depends on relative location (point inside/outside circle, on circumference, point on a produced line), enumerate the possible cases and show how each is covered, or indicate which case is chosen and why it suffices (preferably the hardest case).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use reductio ad absurdum appropriately to rule out impossible configurations
rubrics_metrics.description: Several proofs proceed by assuming an alternative hypothesis and deriving a contradiction (e.g., two circles having the same centre would be impossible, or assumed order relations among equal segments leading to impossibility).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using contradiction, clearly state the assumed contrary hypothesis, derive a clear impossibility (e.g., less than greater, two distinct centres equal), and thereby conclude the original claim. Make sure the contradiction hinges on established facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: When circles touch, centres and contact point are collinear
rubrics_metrics.description: If two circles touch one another (internally or externally), the straight line joining their centres, if produced, will pass through the point of contact (iii.11, iii.12).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prove collinearity of centres and contact point by contradiction or by comparing radii and distances; check/handle the alternative hypotheses that would place the contact off the line of centres and show they lead to impossibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify two-circle configurations by centre distance vs radii
rubrics_metrics.description: Relate the number and nature of common points of two circles to how the distance between their centres compares with the sum and difference of their radii (distance > sum: external disjoint; distance < difference: one inside other; equalities: tangency).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use case distinctions based on OO compared to r + r' and |r - r'|. For each inequality/equality, derive consequences for intersection points, containment, and touching, invoking earlier propositions (iii.7, iii.8 etc.) as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justify existence and uniqueness of tangent constructions from external point
rubrics_metrics.description: Construction (iii.17): from a given external point draw circle centered at that point with radius equal to distance to centre of given circle, draw perpendicular to that radius etc., yielding two equal tangents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide explicit construction steps (choose centre, draw AE, circle with centre A radius AE, draw perpendicular from appropriate point) and prove the constructed line(s) are tangents; show there are exactly two tangents from an external point and they are equal in length and symmetric about the centre line.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove tangent is perpendicular to radius at point of contact (and converses)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a straight line touches a circle and a straight line be joined from the centre to the point of contact, the straight line so joined will be perpendicular to the tangent (iii.18); conversely, a straight line from the point of contact at right angles to the tangent passes through the centre (iii.19).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical proof: assume not perpendicular, draw the perpendicular, compare angles and opposite sides in triangles to derive a contradiction (e.g., less-than/greater-than inconsistency). For converses, use a similar contradiction argument to rule out any other centre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use previously established propositions to complete proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Many of the arguments rely on earlier results (e.g., iii.7, iii.8, i.30, i.20) to handle special positions or to justify extrema of distances; proofs should cite and use such earlier propositions where needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a proof appeals to a fact about shortest/longest straight lines to a circumference, uniqueness of perpendicular bisectors, angles in semicircles, or similar, reference and apply the previously proven proposition rather than re-proving the fact ad hoc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handle assumptions about relative distances in constructions (ensure ordering)
rubrics_metrics.description: Euclid's proofs sometimes assume order relations among points produced on lines (e.g., that C is not within the other circle, or that a produced point is nearer than another). Such ordering must be proved or each alternative shown impossible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a proof requires a point produced beyond another or comparisons of distances, either prove the required ordering or split the argument into the possible orderings and show contradictions in the impossible cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish uniqueness of tangent or contact point (a line touches circle at one point only)
rubrics_metrics.description: Corollary to iii.16 and later remarks assert uniqueness: a straight line meets a circle in at most one point of tangency, and there is but one straight line that touches the circle at a given point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prove uniqueness by showing that a line meeting a circle in two points would fall inside the circle (contradiction), or by using fact that radius to contact is perpendicular and uniqueness of perpendicular from a point.
